Trt_Concerns_Desc:
*   The fire burned rapidly and with great intensity when wind driven, consuming virtually everything in its path. The fire burned range facilities, such as fences and one wildlife guzzler. Primary activities in the fire area include livestock grazing, off road vehicles, camping and hunting. Safety will be considered during seeding and mechanical treatment operations. There are homes (Greenville, UT) and private property (alfalfa and rangeland fields) below the location of the wildfire. These areas have already received impacts from flooding (mud flows) following recent precipitation events.
*   Throughout the burned area, soils are inherently prone to wind erosion and runoff generation. Because the fire consumed soil organic matter and coarse debris in most parts of the burn, the potential for runoff generation from a given precipitation event has increased. Areas of greatest potential impact are the community of Greenville, adjacent agricultural fields and Minersville Reservoir (which is on the State of Utah&$s 303 (d) list of impacted waters).  Decreases in vegetation debris litter cover, increases in runoff generation, and decreases in soil structure and cohesion (due to loss of organic matter) have also increased the susceptibility of soils to erosion from sheet flow. On steeper slopes, there is also increased risk of rill erosion.
*   Greater sage-grouse (Centrocercus urophasianus), a Utah Division of Wildlife Resources and BLM sensitive species are found within the treatment area
*   Covering seed using mechanical methods may negatively impact cultural sites. There are potentially some cultural sites (recorded and unrecorded) within the Greenville Bench Fire Area. The potential for erosion damage and artifact looting is of concern.
*   Noxious weeds are present (Scotch thistle) within the surrounding area of the Greenville Bench Fire.

Treatment_Type: Noxious Weeds: Weed Control - Herbicide Application
Objectives: Control of noxious weeds is consistent with the management plans for the resource and will help protect the ecological integrity, biodiversity, and site productivity of this shrub-steppe plant community.  Treatment of noxious weeds is necessary to comply with Nevada State Laws, to implement the Integrated Weed Management Program of the Elko Field Office, and to be responsible neighbors to the adjacent private landowners.  Working cooperatively with local weed management groups and private landowners will achieve better weed management.
Planned_Implementation: During the implementation of the emergency stabilization plan, treatments and evaluations will be conducted on approximately 2,400 acres (1,200 acres treatments and 1,200 acres evaluations) for noxious weed infestations.  During the implementation of the rehabilitation plan, treatments and evaluations will be conducted on approximately 1,930 acres (965 acres of treatments and 965 acres of evaluations) for 2 years.  Noxious weeds known to exist within the burned area are hoary cress, Russian knapweed, and Scotch thistle.  More infestations may be detected as plants recover from the fire or establish from spread seeds.  Integrated weed treatments will be used including, but may not be limited to, manual and chemical weed control measures.  Manual treatments will be done by grubbing with shovels or hand pulling or chopping off of fruiting structures.  Chemical treatments will be done following all label requirements and conform to the BLM Chemical Pest Control Handbook H-9011-1.  Herbicides, Surfactants, and Dyes used will be approved for use on BLM administered lands and applied following standard safety and operating procedures.  Herbicide application to rangeland sites will be by low pressure backpack sprayer or hand gun from an ATV.  Herbicide application to road right-of-ways will be by vehicle mounted unit or ATV.  No aerial application is planned.

FY 2018:
Discussion: Bromus tectorum (Cheatgrass) was treated aerially through a contract that sprayed in April/May. The contract was only for the low lands and excluded the stream that runs through the fire. In regards to the noxious weeds, in October 2017 funding was placed into an interagency agreement with the National Park Service’s (NPS) Lake Mead National Recreation’s (LAKE) Invasive Plant Management Team (IPMT) for future treatments. They were on the ground treating from August 8th to the 13th.
Results: Acroptilon repens (Russian Knapweed) was the only noxious weed that was treated. The rest of the fire was monitored for noxious weeds and none were found. A total of 592 gallons of chemical was sprayed one the sites with a mix of Weeder 64 and either Tordon 22K or Transline. The Cheatgrass was sprayed and looking at the site later on the chemical had an impact, and there was minimal missed areas. ? Recommendations: Continue to treat for Noxious Weeds
FY 2020:
Discussion: Lake Mead sprayed the fire on August 7th through 9th. They sprayed Russian Knapweed, Hoary Cress (Cardaria draba), and Russian thistle (Salsola Kali). A total of 14.35 total gallons of mix was sprayed. There were 3 different mixes used mix one was habitat and a surfactant, mix 2 was transline and a surfactant and mix 3 was Tordon 22K and a surfactant. Results: Treatments have been effective at reducing noxious weeds within the burned area. Not much growth of Russian thistle during current year, but this is likely due to drought conditions observed within the area. Hoary cress and Russian knapweed were found and spot-treated within the area.

Objectives:
1.) Imazapic: The objective of the Imazapic treatment is to suppress cheatgrass in order to establish the
favorable perennial grasses, forbs, and shrubs into the site. The presence and abundance of the forage
kochia as well as cheatgrass would be compared between years to determine treatment effectiveness.
2.) Fuelbreak: The objective of the treatment is to create a break in the continuity of fuels that will, in the
event of a wildland fire, allow for suppression actions to be conducted safely and reduce overall fire size.
The treatment objectives will be met if there are one and a half forage kochia seedlings per square meter.

Actual_Implementation: The Aerial Imazapic/Aerial Overseed Rock Creek PHMA & GHMA\r\nTreatment was an aerial herbicide application of Imazapic in the fall of 2016
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Density: The Aerial Imazapic/Drill Rock Creek PHMA & GHMA Treatment was an aerial
herbicide application of Imazapic in the fall of 2016, followed by an aerial seeding in the winter
of 2016-2017 and a drill seeding the following winter of 2017-2018. The ground seeding was
applied via rangeland drill to the public burned land in areas selected to be in accordance with
the ecological sites and elevation and was comprised of Snake River Wheatgrass, Bluebunch
Wheatgrass, Siberian Wheatgrass, Gooseberry Leaf Globemallow, Four-wing Saltbush
Sandberg’s Bluegrass. AIM Plots 04 and 05 were monitored in 2019. The four-wing saltbush
establishment is showing reduced progress towards success: there were a recorded average of
0.03 seeded four-wing saltbush plants per square meter in 2018 surveys and none recorded in the
two plots in 2019. The treatment is considered successful when one big sagebrush seedling, one
and a half forb species (yarrow or flax) and one and a half grass seedlings per square meter are
established. Regrowth of Sandberg bluegrass and crested wheatgrass was observed on the plots.
Forb seedlings are displaying reduced establishment success in these sites: 0.80 seeded blue flax
plants per square meter were recorded in 2018 monitoring and none were recorded in the two
plots in 2019. Seeded grasses have are still showing rehabilitation success and are very
successful in third year monitoring: there were an average of 50.34 seeded grasses per square
meter in the treatment area.
Cover: Average foliar canopy cover has decreased to 69.3% in the treatment area. Perennial
grasses have 39.7% cover. Cheatgrass cover had reduced cover (12.5%) in 2017, an intended
positive correlation to the aerial herbicide treatment. Cheatgrass cover more-than doubled, to
27.6%, from 2017 to 2018. The cheatgrass coverage is up to 33.3% at least in the two-plot
average of 2019 monitoring. This level of cheatgrass cover is less cover than all other non-
imazapic treated areas in the Hot Pot rehab area. Native perennial plant regrowth has been
reduced, with perennial grasses at 39.7% cover and perennial forbs at 1.3% cover. Sandberg’s
bluegrass (Poa secunda) cover decreased to 14.7%, while squirreltail (Elymus elymoidies)
improved to 8% cover. Tall tumble mustard cover increased to 7.7% - it appeared to be
hampered initially by the herbicide as it had only 0.8% cover in 2017. Overall, the native and
seeded perennial plant species are competing well against the annual invasive grasses and forbs;
this positively correlated with the aerial herbicide application in the fall of 2016. These results
display a success in the aerial imazapic treatments.
Gaps: Gaps in canopy foliar cover have increased from the second to third growing seasons but
have not reached 2017 levels. The majority of gaps are between 101 and 200cm. Canopy cover
represents less than half of the average 25m transects. These gaps make the site susceptible to
wind and water erosion.

Planned_Implementation:
Invasive Exotic Plants and Noxious Weed Treatments:
Invasive exotic plants are known to occur within the Copper Fire perimeter and in the
surrounding landscape. In order to maximize a successful rehabilitation outcome, the BLM must
strive to reduce both invasive exotic plants and Nevada listed noxious weeds. These species will
often times outcompete desirable native and non-native species and disrupt the overall function
of any given ecosystem. Several examples of invasive exotic plants are known to occur within
the area of the Copper Fire include Bromus tectorum (Cheat Grass), Alyssum desertorum (Desert
Madwort), Halogeton glomeratus (Saltlover), and Lepidium perfoliatum (Clasping Pepperweed).
There were no known Nevada listed noxious weed species found within the fire. Nevada State
Law requires that all populations of noxious weed be treated.
There is an increased potential for these populations to establish and expand within burned areas.
Invasive exotic and noxious weed species can have seeds banks that persist through a burn and
are often times the first species to germinate following a fire. Existing seed sources can be
supplemented by wind, vehicles, and livestock moving through the area. Given the extent of
invasive exotic species populations, especially in the lowland treatment area, there is a limited
potential for recovery without specific invasive exotic and noxious weed species treatments. The
BLM is proposing both chemical and targeted grazing treatments to manage the spread of
invasive exotic and noxious weed species populations.
The BLM generally spot treats populations of noxious weed species and most invasive exotic
species as part of post fire rehabilitation. The BLM will use an approved herbicide mix, which
will be sprayed at a recommended rate. Monitoring and treatments will be funded under this
project for a period of five years.
The BLM will use lmazapic within the fire perimeter to reduce the Cheat Grass, assist the
reseeding measures, and promote native plant recovery. lmazapic is a relatively selective
